robots.name: Boot
robots.teaches: how to get set up from zero, even if you have never coded
robots.personality: Patient and encouraging. Never makes you feel behind.
robots.pitch: Boot gets you from never coded to talking to your first robot, in one sitting. Totally free.
hire: You have never opened a terminal and it looks scary
You want to try AI on your business before spending a dime
You need the five sentences that work for almost anything
You want to know which robot to hire first

lessons.title: What a terminal actually is, and why it is not scary
lessons.summary: A terminal is just a text window where you type and the computer answers, and it is safe to try.
lessons.hook: A terminal is a plain chat window

steps.title: Open the window
steps.note: Search your computer for Terminal, then open it. Brand new? Typing claude will not work yet, because it is not installed. Lesson 2 installs it in one line.
steps.why: You need somewhere to type.
steps.picture: It's a text thread with your computer, like texting a friend who never leaves you on read.

lessons.title: Day one: from never coded to talking to Claude
lessons.summary: Seven steps from zero to your first sentence in Claude Code, on a Mac or a Windows PC.

steps.title: Get the Claude Pro plan
steps.note: The free plan does not include Claude Code. Heavy days can hit your usage limit. That's normal. It resets, and you can move up a plan later if it keeps happening.
steps.why: Claude Code is not in the free plan.
steps.picture: It's a movie ticket. No ticket, no seat, no matter how early you show up.
steps.skip: You install everything, then get turned away. Like showing up at the movies with popcorn but no ticket.

steps.title: Open your terminal
steps.note: It is already on your laptop.
steps.why: Everything you type happens in this window.
steps.picture: It's the front door to your laptop. It was always there, just unlabeled.

platforms.label: Mac
platforms.how: Press Command + Space, type Terminal, press Enter.

platforms.label: Windows PC
platforms.how: Press the Windows key, type PowerShell, press Enter.

steps.title: Paste one line to install
steps.note: Then press Enter and wait. It shows nothing while it downloads. That is normal.
steps.why: One line sets everything up for you.
steps.picture: It's pasting a shopping list into a delivery app. The groceries just show up.
steps.screen_title: Download Claude Code on your desktop.

steps.title: Type claude
steps.note: Close the window, open a new one, then type one word. If it says command not found, close every terminal window, open a fresh one, and try again.
steps.why: The first time, it needs to know it's you.
steps.picture: It's saying the dog's name. One word, and it comes running.
prompts: claude

steps.title: Just talk to it
steps.note: Plain English. Like texting a person.
steps.why: Plain sentences work. No special words needed.
steps.picture: It's directions for a brilliant new hire. Tell them the job, plainly.
prompts: I run a dog training business. Here's what I do every week: [list]. Teach me in low cognitive load where you can help first. One step at a time.

steps.title: Read before you say yes
steps.note: It asks before changing files. Read the ask, then answer.
steps.why: You stay in charge of every change.
steps.picture: Claude is the intern handing you a letter. You sign it, not the intern.
steps.skip: You sign the intern's letter without reading. Your neighbor now has opinions about their fence.
prompts: Before you change anything, ask me first

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Ask it to say what it just did.
steps.why: You sign off, so mistakes get caught early.
steps.picture: It's checking your teeth for spinach before a meeting. Two seconds now, no awkward later.
prompts: Tell me what you just did for me, step by step

lessons.title: Connect your camera roll, texts and voice memos
lessons.summary: Give Claude Code the key to your photos, texts and voice memos on a Mac, then put it to work in one sentence each.

steps.title: Turn on Full Disk Access
steps.note: Open System Settings, then Privacy and Security, then Full Disk Access. Turn on Terminal.
steps.why: Your Mac keeps photos, texts and memos locked until you say so.
steps.picture: It's a hotel key card. The room is there, but the door stays shut until the front desk turns the card on.
steps.skip: Claude says operation not permitted, and you think it's broken. It's not. It just has no key card.
prompts: Can you see my Messages and Voice Memos folders?

steps.title: Quit and reopen Terminal
steps.note: Press Command Q, open Terminal again, and type claude.
steps.why: The new permission only works in a fresh window.
steps.picture: It's restarting the wifi router. Annoying, but it's the fix.
steps.skip: You flip the switch, nothing changes, and you flip it eight more times.
prompts: claude

steps.title: Grab photos from your camera roll
steps.note: Ask for copies. If your Mac asks to let Terminal control Photos, click OK.
steps.why: Copies keep your originals safe.
steps.picture: It's a photocopy. The original stays in the file cabinet.
steps.skip: You scroll your camera roll for twenty minutes, every single time you post.
prompts: Copy my 10 newest photos into a folder on my Desktop called Posts

steps.title: Catch up on your texts
steps.note: Ask it to read a conversation and sum it up.
steps.why: It reads only. Nothing gets sent.
steps.picture: It's the friend who read the whole group chat and tells you the three parts that matter.
steps.skip: You scroll for ten minutes to find one address.
prompts: Read my last 20 texts with Sam and give me a three line summary

steps.title: Turn a voice memo into a to-do list
steps.note: If it asks to install a free tool to write out the audio, read the ask, then say yes.
steps.why: You talk your ideas, and it hands you a list.
steps.picture: It's an assistant taking dictation who never judges the rambling.
steps.skip: Your best idea lives in memo number forty-seven, forever.
prompts: Find my newest voice memo, write it out, and make a to-do list from it

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Set the house rule: read only, and ask before changing, moving or sending anything.
steps.why: Full Disk Access is a big key. You set the rules. You can switch it off any time in the same setting.
steps.picture: You handed over the master key. This is the house rules taped by the door.
prompts: Read only. Ask me before you change, move or send anything.

lessons.title: Your first 5 sentences to try in Claude Code
lessons.summary: Five plain sentences that show a first-time user what Claude Code can do for a small business.

steps.title: Look around
steps.note: Sentences one and two: see files, summarize a PDF.
steps.why: Seeing what is there comes before changing anything.
steps.picture: It's a flashlight in a dark garage. You look first, then you move things.
prompts: What files are on my desktop?

steps.title: Do the busywork
steps.note: Sentences three and four: lists and photo names.
steps.why: Boring jobs are what it does best.
steps.picture: It's a helper who loves alphabetizing the spice rack, and never complains.
prompts: Make a to-do list from these notes. Then rename my photos by date.

steps.title: Ask about your business
steps.note: Sentence five: tell it your real week and ask for a faster way.
steps.why: It gives better ideas when it knows what you do.
steps.picture: Ask it like a brand new hire. Tell them what you do first, or you get random chores.
prompts: Here's my week: I answer client texts, post the class schedule, chase invoices and make flyers. Which one eats the most time, and is there a faster way to do it?

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Read the answers and fix what is wrong.
steps.why: It can be confidently wrong, so you sign off.
steps.picture: It's a dog proudly bringing the wrong shoe. Thank it, then check which shoe.
prompts: Show me what you did and what you were unsure about

lessons.title: Basic safety: you are always the boss
lessons.summary: Claude Code asks first, you can stop it any time, and secrets stay out of the chat.

steps.title: Read the ask first
steps.note: Claude Code asks permission before running commands or changing files.
steps.why: You decide what happens on your computer.
steps.picture: Claude is the intern handing you a letter. You sign it, not the intern.
steps.skip: You sign the intern's letter blind, and your landlord gets a very strange email.
prompts: Before you change any file, ask me first

steps.title: Know the stop key
steps.note: Press the Escape key to stop it in the middle of a task.
steps.why: You can halt anything, any time.
steps.picture: It's the brake pedal. You hope not to need it, but you know where it is.
steps.skip: You watch the robot happily reorganize everything while you hunt for the brake pedal.
prompts: Tidy my desktop files into folders

steps.title: Keep secrets out of chat
steps.note: Never paste passwords or secret keys into the chat.
steps.why: Anyone who sees a key can use your account.
steps.picture: A secret key is your house key. You don't tape it to the front door.
steps.skip: Strangers walk right in, and they eat your snacks.
prompts: How do I log in to my email safely?

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Ask for a draft before anything is sent.
steps.why: Nothing goes out until you read it.
steps.picture: The robot is the intern. You're the one who signs the letter.
steps.skip: Your real client gets an email that was meant to be a joke about llamas.
prompts: Write a draft reply, but do not send it

lessons.title: Save your work before big changes
lessons.summary: Git keeps free save points, so a big change that breaks things is one step from undone.

steps.title: Make a save point
steps.note: Ask it to set up git, then save before big changes.
steps.why: Git is a free tool that keeps save points.
steps.picture: It's a save point in a video game. Lose to the boss, restart at the save.
prompts: Set up git in this folder, then save a save point

steps.title: Go back when it breaks
steps.note: Ask it to go back to the last save point.
steps.why: You undo the mess without starting over.
steps.picture: It's reloading your game. Back at the boss door, health full, no tears.
prompts: Something broke. Go back to the last save point

steps.title: Keep a spare copy
steps.note: Keep a backup copy of important files somewhere else.
steps.why: One broken computer should not end your business.
steps.picture: A backup is the spare key at your neighbor's house.
prompts: Which of my files are most important to back up?

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Ask it to show your save points and the last change.
steps.why: You see the safety net is really there.
steps.picture: It's checking your teeth for spinach. Two seconds now, no awkward later.
prompts: Show me my save points in plain English

lessons.title: Give clear directions, get good results
lessons.summary: Say who it is for, what you want and what good looks like, and the first try gets much closer.

steps.title: Say who, what, and good
steps.note: Say who it is for, what you want, and what good looks like.
steps.why: Clear directions mean fewer do-overs.
steps.picture: It's directions for a brilliant new hire. Say "make it pop" and you get fireworks.
prompts: Write a welcome email for new clients, friendly, under 100 words

steps.title: Give an example
steps.note: Paste or describe one example of what you like.
steps.why: Showing beats explaining every time.
steps.picture: It's showing the barista a photo of the latte you want.
prompts: Write it like this example: Hi Sam, so glad you're here!

steps.title: Let it ask questions
steps.note: For a big job, ask it to ask you questions first.
steps.why: Questions up front save a redo later.
steps.picture: It's a contractor measuring before cutting. Boring for a minute, then perfect.
prompts: This is a big job. Ask me questions before you start

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Read it, then say exactly what to change.
steps.why: Specific fixes beat starting over.
steps.picture: It's a dog proudly bringing the wrong shoe. Thank them, then check which shoe.
prompts: Keep the first paragraph, make the ending shorter and warmer. Remember that I like short warm endings, for every email.

lessons.title: Which robot should you hire first?
lessons.summary: Match your biggest pain to the robot that fixes it, and start with just one.

steps.title: Graphics and videos
steps.note: Graphics take forever? Pixel. Videos never edited? Spielbot.
steps.why: Each robot fixes one job really well.
steps.picture: Pixel is the designer who never sleeps. Spielbot is the editor who skips the intro.
prompts: My graphics take forever. Which robot should I hire?

steps.title: Inbox and money
steps.note: Inbox and bookings eat the day? Tempo. Money questions? Penny.
steps.why: Hand off the work you dread most.
steps.picture: Tempo is the receptionist. Penny is the bookkeeper who loves a balanced book.
prompts: My inbox eats my day. Which robot should I hire?

steps.title: Writing and website
steps.note: Writing sounds robotic? Echo. Website changes? Dot.
steps.why: Your words and your site stay yours.
steps.picture: Echo is the ghostwriter who studied you. Dot is the builder who gets it right once.
prompts: My writing sounds robotic. Which robot should I hire?

steps.title: Research and safety
steps.note: Too many research tabs? Scout. Connecting email or payments? Bouncer first.
steps.why: Lock the door before you hand out keys.
steps.picture: Scout reads the long stuff. Bouncer checks every name on the list at the door.
prompts: I want to connect my email. Which robot comes first?

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Start with one robot, then add more as you go.
steps.why: You learn each one before the next.
steps.picture: Six dogs on six leashes, first time? Start with one.
prompts: Help me pick my first robot from my biggest pain

lessons.title: You're the creative one. Say what you hate.
lessons.summary: The robot obeys. It does not dream. Bring the idea, say what you hate, make it try again, and have it remember.

steps.title: Bring the idea yourself
steps.note: Start with what you want and who it's for. Don't ask it for ideas.
steps.why: The robot is not creative. Give it free rein and you get the same bland thing everyone gets.
steps.picture: It's a brilliant new hire who takes everything literally. Say make it pop and you get fireworks.
steps.skip: You get a flyer that looks like every other AI flyer in town.
prompts: I'm making a flyer for our Saturday pack walk. It's for dog owners who worry their dog will act up in a crowd. It needs to feel calm, not cheesy.

steps.title: Say what you hate
steps.note: Tell it what to never do. Be picky. You won't hurt its feelings.
steps.why: "Make it nice" gets you its idea of nice. Your no's make it yours.
steps.picture: It's ordering a burger. If you hate pickles, you say no pickles. You don't just say make it good.
steps.skip: Emojis, centered everything, and a font you'd never pick.
prompts: No emojis. Don't center everything. That font is ugly, pick a plain one. Less words.

steps.title: Never fix it yourself
steps.note: Don't open another app to fix it by hand. Say what's wrong and make it try again.
steps.why: Every fix you make by hand, it never learns. Every fix it makes, it learns.
steps.picture: It's teaching a dog to sit. If you push the dog into a sit every time, the dog never learns to sit.
steps.skip: You fix the same thing by hand every week, forever.
prompts: The date is too small and the dog photo is cut off. Try again.

steps.title: Don't take the first no
steps.note: If it says it can't, ask it to find another way.
steps.why: Can't often means it hasn't found the way yet. Pushing is how it gets better.
steps.picture: It's a dog at a puzzle toy. Quit after one sniff and there's no treat.
steps.skip: You give up on jobs it could have done in two more tries.
prompts: You said you can't. Find another way and try again.

steps.title: Check your work, then say remember that
steps.note: Look it over. Then tell it to save what you taught it.
steps.why: If you explain yourself every time, you waste time and usage. Saved rules load every time.
steps.picture: It's the recipe card on the fridge. Write it once, same dish every time.
steps.skip: Tomorrow it puts the emojis right back.
prompts: Show me the final. Then remember that: no emojis, no centered text, plain fonts, less words. Save it for every design.

lessons.title: Write down your week before you automate it
lessons.summary: Before you hand anything to a robot, write down how you do things now. Then pick the one job that eats your time and hand off just that.

steps.title: Write down how you do things now
steps.note: List your weekly jobs in plain words. How you make flyers, check email, chase payments.
steps.why: You can't hand off a job you can't describe.
steps.picture: It's writing down the recipe before you hire a cook.
steps.skip: You spend hours poking at AI with no plan.
prompts: Here's my week. I answer client texts, post the class schedule, chase invoices and make flyers. Help me write each one as simple steps.

steps.title: Mark what you hate and what you love
steps.note: Next to each job, say if you hate it or love it.
steps.why: Hand off what drains you. Keep what you love.
steps.picture: It's sorting laundry. Most of it goes in the machine. Your favorite sweater you wash by hand.
steps.skip: You automate the part you enjoy and keep the part you dread.
prompts: I hate posting the schedule and chasing invoices. I love making the flyers. Mark them that way.

steps.title: Ask the three questions
steps.note: For each job you hate: would it still feel like you, would it save time, would it keep the quality?
steps.why: If handing it off makes it fake or worse, don't.
steps.picture: It's a dishwasher. Great for plates. Not for your grandma's china.
steps.skip: You automate something people can tell a robot did.
prompts: For each job I hate: if you did it, would it still feel like me, save me time and keep the quality? Yes or no for each.

steps.title: Pick one job. Just one.
steps.note: Start with the biggest time eater that passed all three questions.
steps.why: Automate one thing, get comfortable, then do the next.
steps.picture: It's walking one dog before you try six leashes at once.
steps.skip: Six half-built automations, and none of them work.
prompts: Pick the one job I should hand off first. Teach me in low cognitive load, one step at a time. Tell me when to come back for step two.

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Read the plan back. Make sure it matches how you really work.
steps.why: It only knows what you told it. You know the rest.
steps.picture: It's checking your teeth for spinach before a meeting.
steps.skip: It builds a plan for a business that isn't quite yours.
prompts: Read my plan back to me in five lines. What did you guess at?

lessons.title: Run a few robots at once: one window, one job
lessons.summary: Write today's priorities, open one terminal window per job, give each one assignment, and check in on all of them.

steps.title: Write today's priorities
steps.note: Before you open anything, write down your top three or four jobs for today.
steps.why: Each job gets its own robot. The list tells you how many to open.
steps.picture: It's a grocery list. Walk in without one and you leave with chips and no milk.
steps.skip: You open windows for everything and forget what half of them are doing.
prompts: My priorities today: a list of all my merch, the trainer pay tracker, and photos for a client's dog. Save that as today.md.

steps.title: Open one window per job
steps.note: On a Mac, press Command N in Terminal for a new window. Type claude in each one.
steps.why: Each window keeps its own chat, so jobs don't get mixed up.
steps.picture: It's one leash per dog. Tangle them together and nobody gets walked.
steps.skip: One chat juggles three jobs and mixes them up.
prompts: claude

steps.title: Give each one an assignment
steps.note: Talk to each window like a person on your team. One job, said plainly.
steps.why: A clear job means it works without you hovering.
steps.picture: It's handing each friend one thing to carry in from the car.
steps.skip: It asks you questions all afternoon instead of working.
prompts: Your only job: make a list of all the merch on my store so I can show a local printer. Ask me if you get stuck.

steps.title: Check in. Don't babysit.
steps.note: Glance at each window now and then. Answer its questions so it can keep going.
steps.why: They're not fully on their own. A quick check keeps them on task.
steps.picture: It's peeking through the oven window. You don't sit in front of it for an hour.
steps.skip: One window sat waiting on a question for two hours.
prompts: Where are you at? What do you need from me?

steps.title: Check your work: who did what
steps.note: At the end, ask each window what it did and what it sent.
steps.why: If something went out twice, you want to know which window did it.
steps.picture: It's counting the dogs before you leave the park.
steps.skip: Something gets sent four times and you can't tell which robot did it.
prompts: List everything you did today and anything you sent or published. Then write a handoff note.

robots.name: Pixel
robots.teaches: how to replace Canva and make on-brand graphics with one sentence
robots.personality: Cheerful, a little picky about fonts.
robots.pitch: Pixel makes your graphics, so you never scroll a template site again.
hire: You make the same post graphic every week by hand
Your posts never look like the same brand twice
You need a flyer for a class or sale by tonight
You want your logo, colors and fonts saved so every graphic matches

lessons.title: Make 3 post graphics in your brand from one sentence
lessons.summary: Describe your brand and your post in one sentence and Claude Code makes three graphics for you.

steps.title: Describe your brand
steps.note: Say your colors, your fonts, and your business.
steps.why: I can only match what you tell me.
steps.picture: It's handing a painter a paint swatch. No swatch, and you get beige.
prompts: I run a dog training business. Use deep green, cream, and a clean serif font.

steps.title: Ask for the post
steps.note: Say what the posts are about and how many.
steps.why: Each post needs its own job.
steps.picture: It's ordering three coffees with names on the cups. Nobody gets the wrong drink.
prompts: Make 3 square Instagram post graphics: one tip, one quote, one class announcement.

steps.title: Say what you hate
steps.note: Tell it what to never do. Be picky. Then ask it to remember.
steps.why: "Make it nice" gets you the same look as every AI post. Your no's make it yours.
steps.picture: It's a swatch of what you'd never wear. Saves a lot of returns.
prompts: No emojis, no centered text, no stock-photo smiles. Remember that for every graphic.

steps.title: Tweak what you see
steps.note: Ask for changes in plain words, like to a designer.
steps.why: Small changes are easy when you say them.
steps.picture: It's telling the hairdresser a little shorter. Say it, and I'll trim it.
prompts: Make the headline bigger and the font lighter on the second one.

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Read every word on every graphic.
steps.why: Typos hide in big headlines.
steps.picture: It's checking your teeth for spinach before a meeting. Two seconds now, no awkward later.
prompts: Show me all three and list any text you changed

lessons.title: Save your brand colors and fonts once so every graphic matches
lessons.summary: Tell Claude Code your brand colors and fonts once and ask it to save them so every graphic matches.

lessons.title: Make a class or sale flyer by tonight
lessons.summary: Go from nothing to a finished, on-brand flyer for a class or sale in one sitting, then check every detail.

lessons.title: Make a flyer people get in three seconds
lessons.summary: Pretty is not the same as clear. Give the flyer one message, one path for the eye, and a face that looks toward the sign-up. Then test it.

steps.title: Make a path for the eye
Point the face at the sign-up
Check your work: the three second test

lessons.title: Rack cards to the printer, without the back and forth
lessons.summary: Have Claude design rack cards with a working QR code, make a print-ready file, and write the email to your local printer. It sends once, after your yes.

steps.title: Check your work, then send once

robots.name: Spielbot
robots.teaches: how to replace CapCut: trims, captions and vertical videos
robots.personality: Thinks every clip is a blockbuster. Then cuts it to the good part.
robots.pitch: Spielbot edits your videos, so one recording turns into a week of posts.
hire: You record great videos and never get around to editing them
You spend an hour adding captions by hand
You want one long video cut into three short ones
You need vertical versions for TikTok and Reels

lessons.title: Trim a clip and add captions with one sentence
lessons.summary: Ask Claude to trim a video and add captions in plain English, no editing app needed.

steps.title: Name your clip
steps.note: Say which video and how much to keep.
steps.why: I can't cut a clip I can't find.
steps.picture: It's telling a barber exactly how much to take off, not just a little.
prompts: Trim tour.mp4 on my desktop down to the best thirty seconds.

steps.title: Ask for captions
steps.note: Describe how you want them to look.
steps.why: Most people watch with the sound off.
steps.picture: It's a movie with subtitles. Nobody at the airport hears your video.
prompts: Now add big, easy to read captions to that shorter clip.

steps.title: Fix what looks off
steps.note: Ask for changes in plain words.
steps.why: Small tweaks are cheaper than starting over.
steps.picture: It's asking the barber to take a little more off the left, not a new head.
prompts: The captions are too small. Make them bigger and move them up.

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Watch the whole clip before you post it.
steps.why: I can miss a typo or a bad cut.
steps.picture: It's checking your teeth for spinach before the meeting. Two seconds now, no awkward later.
prompts: Show me where you cut, and read me the captions word for word.

lessons.title: Turn one long video into three short ones
lessons.summary: Ask Claude to find the best moments in one long video and cut them into three short clips.

lessons.title: Turn one video into a vertical post with captions
lessons.summary: Reshape one finished video for TikTok and Reels, keep the best part in frame, and add captions that are easy to read.

lessons.title: Find your best clips without scrolling your camera roll
lessons.summary: Have Claude pull every clip of one subject from your camera roll, swipe keep or skip, learn what your best posts had in common, and caption the keepers.

steps.title: Add one line on the front

lessons.title: Make an event hype video from clips you already have
lessons.summary: Pull the best clips from last year's event, cut a short vertical video with your own voice and captions, and end with one clear ask.
lessons.hook: Last year's clips. This year's hype.

steps.title: Use your voice, not a robot voice

robots.name: Bouncer
robots.teaches: how to keep your secret keys, passwords and accounts safe, and set the rules your assistant can never break
robots.personality: Friendly but firm. Checks every name on the list.
robots.catchphrase: Not on the list? Not getting in.
robots.pitch: Bouncer guards your accounts and secret keys, so nothing gets in or goes out without your OK.
hire: You're about to connect AI to your email, payments or website
You're not sure where your passwords and keys should live
You want rules your assistant can never break, like never send without asking
You want to sleep at night while robots work for you

lessons.title: What an API key is, and the 3 rules for keeping it safe
lessons.summary: An API key is a secret password that lets one app use another, and three simple rules keep yours safe.
lessons.hook: An API key is a secret password

steps.title: Never paste it in public
steps.note: Not in a chat, a post, or a screenshot.
steps.why: Anyone who sees it can use your account.
steps.picture: It's your house key. You don't tape it to the front door.
steps.skip: You taped your house key to the front door. Strangers drop by, and they don't bring snacks.
prompts: Is it safe to paste my API key into a post?

steps.title: Use a private file
steps.note: Store it in a file your assistant reads.
steps.why: A private file keeps it out of sight.
steps.picture: It's a locked drawer inside the house, not the doormat everyone checks.
steps.skip: The key sits under the doormat. Everyone checks the doormat.
prompts: Please store my key in a private dot env file, and keep it out of anything I share.

steps.title: If it leaks, replace it
steps.note: Turn it off, then make a new one.
steps.why: A new key makes the old one useless.
steps.picture: It's changing the locks after losing your keys. The finder gets a useless key.
steps.skip: You never change the locks. The finder keeps visiting, and now has a favorite chair.
prompts: How do I turn off a leaked key and make a new one?

steps.title: Check your work
steps.note: Ask where your key lives, then look.
steps.why: You sign off that no key is sitting in the open.
steps.picture: It's checking your teeth for spinach before a meeting. Two seconds now, no awkward later.
